# The Value of Disagreement: Why Good Meetings Don't End in Consensus

There is a common belief, woven deep into how most organizations operate, that a successful meeting is one where everyone leaves the room nodding. We celebrate alignment. We praise teams that "get on the same page." A meeting that ends in consensus feels productive, harmonious, finished. A meeting that ends in argument feels like a failure—something went wrong, someone managed the room poorly, someone let things get off track.

But this instinct deserves scrutiny. Agreement, it turns out, is not always a sign that understanding has been achieved. Sometimes it is a sign that understanding has been avoided. People nod for many reasons: because they are tired, because they are intimidated, because the ambiguity of the discussion lets each person walk out believing the group endorsed *their* interpretation of what was decided. The warm glow of consensus can be a mirage. The real work of thinking together often happens not when a group converges, but when it learns to disagree well.
